scenes.text: A professor gave his whole class the same personality reading, and they said it fit them almost perfectly.
In the late nineteen forties, psychologist Bertram Forer gave thirty-nine students a personality test.
A week later, each student got what they thought was their own personal profile.
But every single student received the same text.
Forer had put it together mostly from astrology writing.
It said things like, you have a great need for other people to like and admire you.
And, you have a tendency to be critical of yourself.
On a scale from zero to five, the students rated it above four for accuracy, on average.
This is now called the Forer effect, or the Barnum effect.
Psychologist Paul Meehl named it after showman P. T. Barnum in nineteen fifty-six.
It works best when the statements are vague and mostly flattering.
It works even better when we think an expert made it just for us.
That helps explain why horoscopes, fortune tellers and online personality quizzes can feel so accurate.
Next time a reading feels spot on, ask if it would fit anyone.
Have you ever had a horoscope that felt a little too accurate? Tell me below.

title: Why horoscopes feel scarily accurate 🔮
caption: Psychologist Bertram Forer gave 39 students the same 'personal' profile, and they rated it above 4 out of 5 for accuracy. It's called the Barnum effect, and it's why vague readings feel made for you.
